newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's health insurance sector growing rapidly.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's health insurance sector growing rapidly.

text.p: Private health insurance will continue its strong growth in Turkey as consumers lose confidence in the state-funded social security system and put their savings into private insurance plans.

"Inefficiency in the social security system raises (the) need for health insurance coverage, especially for those who are paid over the average," Ali Behlil, general manager at Halk Sigorta's life subsidiary HalkYasam, told Reuters.
According to Treasury figures, insurance sector premiums jumped 106 percent to 54.33 trillion lira in the first six month of 1996, when compared with the same 1995 period.

Health insurance made up 3.6 trillion lira, or 6.6 percent of the overall premiums in the first half, up from 4.67 percent a year ago, while life insurance made up 7.7 trillion lira, or 14.22 percent, up from 13.1 percent a year ago.

"The main reason behind the sharp growth in health insurance sector is that people's very few fundamental social security needs were met until 1990s. We expect this growth to continue in the future," Behlil said.
Officials said the growth potential in both health and life insurance is high because only a small minority of the country's more than 60 million population is insured.
"The end-1997 forecast is that life premiums will reach 25 trillion and health premiums 15 trillion," said Emre Ilgazer, general manager of AkHayat (life).

Shares of fire, accident and transportation branches in total premiums fell slightly in the first half of 1996, compared with a year ago, but accident insurance still led with a 44.35 percent share, followed by fire with an 18.5 percent share.

According to unofficial nine-month 1996 figures provided by sector officials, overall premiums reached 85 trillion lira while health premiums surged by 178 percent and life premiums by 122 percent from the first nine months of 1995.

The Treasury put new life insurance regulations into effect on December 9 with the aim of developing a source of long-term funds. It also aimed to prevent the erosion of premiums from inflation that currently runs at around 80 percent.
Officials said the rising number of companies in the whole sector also had led to severe competition in prices.

"There is also stiff competition among health insurance firms. Premium calculations should be made very carefully due to rising health costs. That hurts companies' profits," said Candan Ozcan, assistant general manager at Emek Hayat, life branch of Emek Sigorta.
Turkey plans to revise insurance regulations to tighten control in the sector by raising the minimum initial capital of insurance companies to 500 billion lira from 350 billion.
